analysis.investment_thesis: Eris has a genuine structural moat in chronic therapies (diabetes, CVD) riding India's disease burden tailwind, with impressive 19.2% revenue and 20.6% EBITDA CAGR over nine years. However, an acquisition-fueled debt binge has caused finance costs to explode 100x — from ₹2 Cr to ₹231 Cr — collapsing net profit back below FY2022 levels, making the current 45x P/E unjustifiable.
key_strengths: Chronic therapy franchise (anti-diabetes, cardiovascular) with structural Indian tailwind — ₹1,033 Cr EBITDA in FY2025, 26% operating margins
Consistent OCF generation — 5/5 years positive, FY2025 OCF surged to ₹1,065 Cr with FCF of ₹910 Cr signaling post-acquisition free cash inflection
Promoter holding steady at 53.92% with 18-year operating track record in branded generics from Ahmedabad
key_risks: Debt exploded from near-zero to ₹2,478 Cr; finance costs of ₹231 Cr in FY2025 are gutting net profit — ROE collapsed to 12.9%, well below my 20% benchmark
Net profit (₹375 Cr) in FY2025 is actually lower than FY2022 (₹406 Cr) despite revenue nearly doubling — acquisition amortization and interest are destroying shareholder value at the bottom line
Valuation at 45x trailing P/E with sub-13% ROE offers no margin of safety; even forward P/E of 28.6x requires aggressive earnings recovery assumptions
red_flags: Net profit CAGR of 12% vs revenue CAGR of 19.2% — persistent and widening divergence over the last 3 years
Finance costs 100x'd in 4 years (₹2 Cr → ₹231 Cr): acquisition debt is the dominant P&L driver, not operating performance
Total assets ballooned 4.8x (₹1,502 Cr → ₹7,160 Cr) in 5 years — acquisition-heavy capital deployment with unclear ROIC on acquired businesses
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Eris has built a compelling chronic-care franchise over 18 years — the kind of India consumption story I love. Anti-diabetes and cardiovascular are not fads; they are inevitable outcomes of India's urbanization and dietary shifts over the next two decades. Revenue compounding at 19.2% and EBITDA at 20.6% over nine years is genuinely excellent, and the FY2025 operating cash flow jump to ₹1,065 Cr tells me the acquired businesses are finally contributing operating leverage. The ₹910 Cr FCF in FY2025 — if sustained — gives them the firepower to deleverage ₹2,400 Cr of debt within 3 years.

The problem is the price at which I'm being asked to own this story. Net profit has actually gone backwards: ₹406 Cr in FY2022 down to ₹375 Cr in FY2025, while the market charges me 45x for it. Finance costs of ₹231 Cr consumed a quarter of EBITDA in FY2025; until this burden visibly falls, the ROE of 12.9% and ROCE of 12.2% remain well below my 15-20% hurdle. I would revisit eagerly if debt falls below ₹1,000 Cr, ROE crosses 18%, and the stock re-rates to 25-30x forward earnings — that would be a genuine entry point for a 5-year hold on this excellent therapeutic franchise.
